Psychology, Humanities & Social Sciences
Research & Analysis
Interdisciplinary Studies

A Researcher investigates questions, analyses evidence, evaluates existing knowledge, and develops reliable conclusions. Researchers may work in psychology, sociology, economics, political science, history, literature, education, public policy, cultural studies, or interdisciplinary fields.

A Liberal Arts & Sciences degree with a flexible major-minor structure can help students explore different disciplines while developing research, analytical, writing, and communication skills. To become competitive for a research role, students should select a clear research focus and gain practical experience with appropriate research methods.

Stage 1 — Exploration and academic foundations

blocks.label: Suggested period
blocks.text: First year
Learn

items.text: Explore disciplines such as psychology, sociology, economics, history, political science and literature.
Develop academic reading, critical thinking and structured writing.
Understand the difference between a claim, an opinion and evidence.
Learn basic research questions, hypotheses and conceptual frameworks.
Build foundations in statistics, data interpretation and information literacy.
Use academic search tools to locate credible research.
Practise citations, referencing and academic integrity.

blocks.text: Practical activities

items.text: Compare how two disciplines investigate the same issue.
Summarise a small collection of peer-reviewed articles.
Write a short literature-based essay with properly cited sources.
Identify limitations and possible biases in a published study.

blocks.label: Milestone
blocks.text: Identify a promising subject area and communicate evidence-based arguments clearly.
Stage 2 — Research methodology and specialisation

blocks.label: Suggested period
blocks.text: Second year
Learn

items.text: Research design and the formulation of researchable questions.
Literature reviews and critical synthesis.

blocks.label: Qualitative methods
blocks.text: interviews, observation, focus groups and document analysis.

blocks.label: Quantitative methods
blocks.text: surveys, descriptive statistics and introductory hypothesis testing.

items.text: Sampling, measurement, reliability, validity and potential bias.
Research ethics, informed consent and confidentiality.
Reference management and organised research notes.

blocks.text: Practical activities

items.text: Develop a small research proposal.
Create a literature matrix summarising sources and findings.
Design a questionnaire or qualitative interview guide.
Prepare a research plan that includes ethical considerations.

blocks.label: Milestone
blocks.text: Design a feasible research study with a clear question, suitable method and ethical safeguards.
Stage 3 — Data collection and analysis

blocks.label: Suggested period
blocks.text: Third year
Learn

items.text: Quantitative data cleaning and descriptive analysis.
Introductory inferential statistics and interpretation of uncertainty.
Qualitative coding, thematic analysis and systematic note-taking.
Research documentation and data management.
Spreadsheet analysis and introductory statistical software.
Academic argumentation, evidence synthesis and research limitations.
Reproducible workflows and transparent reporting.

blocks.text: Practical activities

items.text: Conduct a small, supervised study using an appropriate dataset or approved research method.
Analyse a public dataset or a permitted collection of documents.
Compare findings with existing literature.
Write a report that distinguishes observed results from interpretation.

blocks.label: Milestone
blocks.text: Complete a small research project and explain how the methods support the conclusions.
Stage 4 — Independent project and career preparation

blocks.label: Suggested period
blocks.text: Final learning phase
Learn

items.text: Advanced methods relevant to the chosen discipline.
Research proposal development and project planning.
Literature synthesis and evidence evaluation.
Academic writing, editing, citations and presentation.
Research ethics and discipline-specific data protection.
Project documentation and research communication for different audiences.
Appropriate digital tools for qualitative or quantitative analysis.

blocks.text: Practical activities

items.text: Complete a capstone research project under appropriate supervision.
Present findings through a poster, seminar or written report.
Seek a research internship or assistantship.
Prepare a portfolio of research writing, methods and analytical work.

blocks.label: Milestone
blocks.text: Demonstrate readiness for entry-level research support roles or postgraduate research preparation.
A flexible degree is most effective when the student combines a main discipline with a complementary minor and appropriate methods training.
Psychology and Behavioural Research
Investigate human behaviour, learning, attitudes, decision-making and social interaction.

blocks.label: Focus

Sociology and Public Policy Research

blocks.label: Focus
blocks.text: surveys, interviews, policy analysis, descriptive statistics and evidence synthesis.
History, Literature and Cultural Research
Analyse historical records, texts, cultural practices, narratives and intellectual traditions.

blocks.label: Focus
blocks.text: archival methods, textual analysis, source criticism, interpretation and academic writing.
Economics and Political Research
Investigate markets, institutions, political behaviour, governance and economic or policy outcomes.

blocks.label: Focus

Interdisciplinary Research
Combine perspectives from two or more disciplines to investigate complex questions such as technology and society, education, sustainability or digital culture.

blocks.label: Focus

blocks.text: Tool selection should follow the research question, discipline, budget and institution's policies. A researcher does not need every tool listed above.
Choose projects appropriate to the student's major, research methods training and available supervision.

blocks.label: Project 1
blocks.text: Structured literature review

blocks.label: Level
blocks.text: Beginner

blocks.label: Build
blocks.text: Investigate a focused question by reviewing a defined set of relevant academic papers.

blocks.label: Demonstrate
blocks.text: Search strategy, source selection, comparison of methods, synthesis of findings and identification of gaps.

blocks.label: Deliverables
blocks.text: Research question, search log, literature matrix, cited review and limitations section.

blocks.label: Project 2
blocks.text: Survey-based research study

blocks.label: Level
blocks.text: Intermediate

blocks.label: Build
blocks.text: Design a small survey to investigate an appropriate question, subject to relevant ethical approval and supervision.

blocks.label: Demonstrate
blocks.text: Questionnaire design, sampling considerations, data cleaning, descriptive statistics and responsible interpretation.

blocks.label: Deliverables
blocks.text: Research protocol, survey instrument, anonymised dataset where permitted, analysis and report.

blocks.label: Ethics note
blocks.text: Obtain the necessary approvals and informed consent before collecting data from participants. Avoid collecting unnecessary personal or sensitive information.

blocks.label: Project 3
blocks.text: Policy or historical document analysis

blocks.label: Level
blocks.text: Intermediate

blocks.label: Build
blocks.text: Analyse a collection of public policy documents, historical sources or other suitable texts to answer a defined research question.

blocks.label: Demonstrate
blocks.text: Source evaluation, coding framework, thematic or comparative analysis, citations and evidence-based argumentation.

blocks.label: Deliverables
blocks.text: Source register, analytical framework, findings report and discussion of source limitations.

blocks.label: Project 4
blocks.text: Public-data research report

blocks.label: Level
blocks.text: Advanced

blocks.label: Build
blocks.text: Use an appropriate public dataset to investigate a social, economic, educational or demographic question.

blocks.label: Demonstrate
blocks.text: Data cleaning, descriptive analysis, visualisation, interpretation of uncertainty and critical discussion.

blocks.label: Deliverables
blocks.text: Reproducible analysis, data-source notes, charts, a research report and limitations.

blocks.label: Research standard
blocks.text: Correlation alone does not establish causation. State clearly what the available data can and cannot support.

For each project, document the research question, rationale, source material, methodology, findings, limitations, references and ethical considerations. Never invent data, sources, interviews or findings.
Begin applying after completing at least one well-documented research project and learning how to review and cite academic literature.

Explain how your academic interests relate to the project's question.
Seek supervised opportunities when a role involves human participants or sensitive data.

blocks.text: Job titles and eligibility vary. Some positions accept graduates from multiple disciplines, while others require a specific major, language proficiency, statistical skills or postgraduate training.
Possible postgraduate directions include:

items.text: MA or MSc in Psychology, Sociology, Economics, Political Science or another relevant subject.
Master's in Public Policy or Development Studies.
Master's in Education Research.
Master's in History, Literature or Cultural Studies.
Master's in Social Research Methods.
Master's in Applied Statistics or Social Data Science.
MPhil or PhD pathways where available and permitted under applicable institutional regulations.

blocks.text: Admission requirements differ substantially. Psychology research programmes may have subject prerequisites; quantitative research programmes may expect statistics or mathematics; humanities programmes may prioritise disciplinary preparation and writing samples. Verify the requirements of each institution before applying.
Stage 1 — Research Intern or Assistant
Support literature searches, data collection, documentation and basic analysis.
Stage 2 — Research Associate or Junior Researcher
Manage defined research tasks, conduct analyses and contribute to reports or publications.
Stage 3 — Researcher or Research Specialist
Develop subject expertise, design parts of studies and lead analytical work within a project.
Stage 4 — Senior Researcher, Principal Investigator or Research Lead
Lead research programmes, manage teams and funding, and guide research strategy where qualifications and experience permit.

Progression depends on the discipline, research outputs, methodological expertise, funding and employer requirements. Principal investigator and academic positions commonly require advanced qualifications and a substantial record of research.

Emerging opportunities do not remove the need for sound methodology, critical evaluation, transparency and responsible handling of research data.

A job-ready graduate should be able to:

items.text: Identify a meaningful research question and explain its importance.
Locate, assess and synthesise credible sources.
Select appropriate research methods and explain why they fit the question.
Collect or organise evidence responsibly.
Analyse qualitative or quantitative material accurately.
Interpret findings without overstating what the evidence supports.
Write clear, well-referenced reports and present conclusions.
Follow research ethics, confidentiality and data-management requirements.
Demonstrate practical ability through a research portfolio and supervised experience.

blocks.label: Recommended priority
blocks.text: Choose a clear research specialisation early, then develop research methodology, academic writing and data-analysis skills alongside the major-minor curriculum. Complete at least one substantial, well-documented project and seek supervised research experience. A strong writing sample, transparent methodology and careful interpretation of evidence will help demonstrate readiness for entry-level research roles.
